overview: This entry represents the modern Republic of Austria, not the medieval duchy or the Habsburg Empire. The republic began in 1918; the map starts in 1920. Its history includes democratic innovation, authoritarian rule, Nazi annexation, persecution, and the restoration of a democratic state after the Second World War.

periods.title: Republic and authoritarian rupture
periods.summary: The 1920 constitution organized the republic. Parliamentary democracy was destroyed before Nazi Germany annexed Austria in 1938.

periods.title: Annexation and Nazi rule
periods.summary: Austria lost independent statehood. Nazi institutions carried out persecution, forced labor and murder, including at Mauthausen.

periods.title: The restored republic
periods.summary: A provisional government proclaimed independence in 1945. Democratic institutions were restored, and the postwar republic continued through the following decades.

items.text: Women first voted in an Austrian national election in 1919, and eight women entered the new assembly. Their presence changed who could participate directly in lawmaking. The right to vote preceded this map’s 1920 starting point and belongs to the republic’s founding story.

In 1920, women legislators including Hildegard Burjan and Anna Boschek helped secure legal protections for domestic servants, including rest and holidays. Household work was part of political debate. A kitchen or nursery could be a workplace whose conditions required rules, just as a factory did.

Article 1 of the constitution reads: “Österreich ist eine demokratische Republik. Ihr Recht geht vom Volk aus.” Translation: “Austria is a democratic republic. Its law emanates from the people.” The German text is a concise statement of where public authority is meant to come from.

Vienna’s municipal housing program emphasized light, air and practical services. Apartments included their own toilets and water points, while developments could provide kindergartens, gardens and bathing facilities. Those details show how city policy tried to improve ordinary routines, including some of the least glamorous necessities.

Karl-Marx-Hof, built in 1927 to 1930, had communal laundries and two bathhouses. Having water inside an apartment did not necessarily mean having a private bathroom. Laundry and bath facilities shared across the complex made domestic work part of the development’s collective infrastructure.

The republic’s constitutional democracy did not run uninterrupted between the wars. An authoritarian regime replaced it in 1934, before Nazi annexation in 1938. These were distinct political ruptures; treating the whole period as ordinary parliamentary government would hide how rights and institutions were dismantled.

The Nazis established Mauthausen concentration camp in 1938. Prisoners were forced to build the camp and work in the quarry, and the camp system became a site of mass murder. United States troops liberated it on 5 May 1945. Its history belongs centrally to Austria’s past.

On 27 April 1945, a provisional government declared Austria independent again. Recognition by the western Allies followed in October, and elections took place in November. Rebuilding a state involved negotiation and institutions as well as a declaration on paper.

Postwar leaders often presented Austria only as a victim of Nazi Germany. The history museum explains how that account obscured Austrian participation and responsibility. Remembering annexation must therefore be accompanied by attention to people who supported persecution, as well as those who suffered or resisted.

The State Treaty signed in May 1955 restored full independence, but neutrality was not written into that treaty. Parliament adopted a separate neutrality law on 26 October. Two events often remembered together had different legal forms and dates.

Austria introduced its schoolbook program in 1972 to help families obtain learning materials. Textbooks became an explicit part of education policy and household support. The program’s history includes changing arrangements, so its founding should not be read as proof that every later year had identical rules.

The mother-and-child health record introduced in 1974 organized preventive examinations during pregnancy and childhood. It later became the parent-child record. This is an example of health administration following a family across stages of life, rather than a claim that one booklet alone produced better health.

After a national referendum in 1994, Austria joined the European Union on 1 January 1995. That decision connected the republic more closely with shared European institutions. Joining the union was a change in international relationships, not the disappearance of Austrian statehood.

Anton Zeilinger shared the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics for experimental work involving entangled photons and quantum information. His affiliations included the University of Vienna and the Austrian Academy of Sciences. The prize recognizes international scientific work; quantum experiments do not mean people can be teleported like characters in a cartoon.

ending.text: The democratic republic re-established after 1945 continues. Its earlier loss of independence in 1938 is a major historical interruption, not an ending that should be assigned to the present-day state. The open-ended map entry refers to this modern republic.
